source.title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning

accepted.question_text: How should the federated learning community define standard evaluation metrics and establish benchmark datasets that are appropriate for the major deployment settings, especially cross-device and cross-silo federated learning, so that proposed methods can be compared on realistic and broadly accepted criteria rather than ad hoc simulations?

evidence.quote: Developing standard evaluation metrics and establishing standard benchmark datasets for different federated learning settings (cross-device and cross-silo) remain highly important directions for ongoing work.

accepted.question_text: In fully decentralized federated learning without a central coordinator, how can stochastic-gradient-based training for deep models be made robust to temporary client unavailability, client dropout and joining, message loss, non-IID client data, heterogeneous update frequencies, and communication-topology choices, while still achieving good practical convergence time?

evidence.quote: Fully decentralized algorithms for learning should be robust to the limited availability of the clients (with clients temporarily unavailable, dropping out or joining during the execution) and limited reliability of the network (with possible message drops). While for the special case of generalized linear models, schemes using the duality structure could enable some of these desired robustness properties [231], for the case of deep learning and SGD this remains an open question. ... Additional open research questions concern non-IID data distributions, update frequencies, efﬁcient communication patterns and practical convergence time [443].

accepted.question_text: For cross-silo federated learning, what formal privacy notion should be optimized in realistic deployments, especially when other participating silos may be a more important threat than the outside world and when each silo may represent many end users whose privacy may need to be protected at the user level?

evidence.quote: On the other hand, for a practically persuasive claim, we would usually need a notion of local differential privacy, as the potential threat from other clients is likely to be more important. In cases when the clients are not considered a signiﬁcant threat, each client could control the data from a number of their respective users, and a formal privacy guarantee might be needed on such user-level basis. Depending on application, other objectives could be worth pursuing. This area has not been systematically explored.

accepted.question_text: Can split learning be parallelized effectively on resource-constrained edge devices so that different parts of the split computation can run with lower centralized training time while remaining practical in federated deployments?

evidence.quote: However, it is still an open question to explore such parallelization of split learning on edge devices.

accepted.question_text: What formal privacy guarantees can be proved for split learning, including guarantees that account for the information leaked by communicated activations or smashed data from clients to the server?

evidence.quote: Overall, much of the discussion in Section 4 is relevant here as well, and analysis providing formal privacy guarantees speciﬁcally for split learning is still an open problem.

accepted.question_text: How can researchers characterize the real cross-client distribution shifts that appear in real-world federated datasets, and use that understanding to build controlled but realistic non-IID benchmarks that stress-test algorithms under the kinds of heterogeneity seen in deployment?

evidence.quote: Real-world federated learning datasets likely contain a mixture of these effects, and the characterization of cross-client differences in real-world partitioned datasets is an important open question. ... A better understanding of the nature of real-world non-IID datasets will allow for the construction of controlled but realistic non-IID datasets for testing algorithms and assessing their resilience to different degrees of client heterogeneity.

accepted.question_text: How should a federated optimization system choose the number of local client updates before aggregation, and potentially the aggregation rule itself, so that the resulting training process achieves the best wall-clock convergence rather than merely good iteration complexity?

evidence.quote: How then to chooseK? Performing more local updates at the clients will increase the divergence between the resulting local models at the clients, before they are averaged. ... The optimal number of local updates strikes a balance between these two phenomena and achieves the fastest error versus wallclock time convergence. ... However, it is unclear whether this aggregation method will result in the fastest error convergence.

accepted.question_text: Can the multi-task or lifelong-learning perspective used for personalization and privacy in federated learning be extended to other phenomena such as concept drift, and can non-parameter-transfer lifelong-learning methods such as ProtoNets be made useful in federated learning?

evidence.quote: Several challenging FL topics including personalization and privacy have begun to be studied in this multi-task/LTL framework [270, 250, 299]. Is it possible for other issues such as concept drift to also be analyzed in this way, for example as a problem in lifelong learning [420]? • Can non-parameter transfer LTL algorithms, such as ProtoNets [425], be of use for FL?

accepted.question_text: Under what data-distribution conditions does a single global federated model outperform independently trained per-client models, how much gain should be expected, and can personalization methods be given guarantees that match or exceed both the purely local baseline and the shared global baseline?

evidence.quote: Thus, a natural theoretical question is to determine under what conditions the shared global model is better than independent per-device models. Suppose we train a model hk for each client k, using the sample of size mk available from that client. Can we guarantee that the model hFL learned via federated learning is at least as accurate as hk when used for client k? Can we quantify how much improvement can be expected via federated leaning? And can we develop personalization strategies with theoretical guarantees that at least match the performance of both natural baselines (hk and hFL)?

accepted.question_text: What privacy-preserving debugging and interpretability methods can answer practical machine-learning workflow questions on decentralized user data, such as inspecting failure cases, outliers, or bias, and how can differentially private federated generative models be improved enough to support those uses faithfully?

evidence.quote: Developing privacy-preserving techniques to answer such questions on decentralized data is a major open problem. ... However, many open questions remain (see discussion in [31]), in particular the development of algorithms that improve the ﬁdelity of FL DP generative models.

accepted.question_text: Can communication in federated learning be reduced substantially further, and what are the practical optimal trade-offs between communication cost and model accuracy once the optimization algorithm is taken into account rather than abstracted away?

evidence.quote: However, it remains unclear if communication cost can be further reduced, and whether any of these methods or their combinations can come close to providing optimal trade-offs between communication and accuracy in federated learning. ... It remains an open direction to leverage such statistical approaches to inform practical training methods.

accepted.question_text: How can compression schemes for federated model updates be designed so that they remain effective while also being compatible with secure aggregation protocols and with differentially private noise-addition mechanisms?

evidence.quote: Many algorithms used in federated learning such as Secure Aggregation [79] and mechanisms of adding noise to achieve differential privacy [3, 338] are not designed to work with compressed or quantized communications. ... Joint design of compression methods that are compatible with Secure Aggregation, or for which differential privacy guarantees can be obtained, is thus a valuable open problem.

accepted.question_text: If homomorphic encryption is used inside federated learning, who should hold the decryption key, and what trust structure or threshold-encryption design can preserve client privacy without assuming an unrealistic permanently trusted external decryptor?

evidence.quote: When considering the use of HE in the FL setting, questions immediately arise about who holds the secret key of the scheme. ... However, most HE schemes require that the secret keys be renewed often ... Moreover, the availability of a trusted non-colluding party is not standard in the FL setting.

accepted.question_text: Can interactive zero-knowledge proofs or non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs be made efficient enough for federated learning, both for proving properties of client inputs to the server and for client-side verification tasks that depend on information from multiple participants?

evidence.quote: Using interactive ZKP systems and NIZKs efﬁciently in the context of FL remains a challenging open question. In such a setting, NIZKs may enable to prove to the server properties about the client’s inputs. In the setting where the veriﬁer is the client, it will be challenging to create a trustworthy statement to verify as it involves input from other clients.

accepted.question_text: What are the fundamental privacy-accuracy trade-offs for user-level differential privacy in federated learning when users contribute highly unequal amounts of data, and how should user contributions be clipped or bounded adaptively in that setting?

evidence.quote: Hence, similar to recent works on user-level DP in the central model [21], ﬁguring out how to adaptively bound the contributions of users and clip the model parameters remains an interesting research direction [446, 377]. More broadly, unlike record-level DP where fundamental trade-offs between accuracy and privacy are well understood for a variety of canonical learning and estimation tasks, user-level DP is fundamentally less understood ... Thus, more work needs to be done to better understand the fundamental trade-offs in this emerging setting of DP.

accepted.question_text: Do privacy-amplification-by-iteration results known for convex optimization extend to the non-convex federated-learning setting, and can practical protocols provide formal privacy guarantees despite dynamic user eligibility, local participation decisions, and mid-protocol dropout?

evidence.quote: This “privacy ampliﬁcation via iteration” setting has been recently studied by Feldman et al. [185] for convex optimization problems. However, it is unclear whether or not the results in [185] can be carried over to the non-convex setting. ... It is therefore important to investigate and design protocols that: (1) are robust to nature’s choice (user availability and dropout), (2) are self-accounting, in that the server can compute a tight (ε,δ) guarantee using only information available via the protocol, (3) rely on local participation decision ... and (4) achieve good privacy-utility trade-offs.

accepted.question_text: How can secure aggregation be made simultaneously efficient, robust, and privacy-preserving when the server may be stronger than semi-honest, when per-round aggregates may leak information, when sparse vectors must be aggregated efficiently, and when client inputs must be checked for well-formedness?

evidence.quote: However, this approach has several limitations: (a) it assumes a semi-honest server (only in the private key infrastructure phase), (b) it allows the server to see the per-round aggregates (which may still leak information), (c) it is not efﬁcient for sparse vector aggregation, and (d) it lacks the ability to enforce well-formedness of client inputs. It is an open question how to construct an efﬁcient and robust secure aggregation protocol that addresses all of these challenges.

accepted.question_text: Is it possible to perform communication-efficient federated training of sub-models while preserving the privacy of which sub-model each client is updating, and what sparsity regimes, private retrieval mechanisms, and secure aggregation variants would make that practical?

evidence.quote: However, when deploying federated learning, communication efﬁciency is often a signiﬁcant concern, leading to the question of whether we can achieve communication-efﬁcient sub-model training. ... Is it possible to achieve communication-efﬁcient sub-model federated learning while also keeping the client’s sub-model choice private?

accepted.question_text: Can federated learning adopt a realistic trust model in which the server is trusted but continuously verifiable, including explicit assumptions about what fraction of clients might be compromised and whether simultaneous compromise of server and many devices should be assumed?

evidence.quote: For example, what is a reasonable fraction of clients to assume might be compromised by an adversary? Is it likely for an adversary to be able to compromise both the server and a large number of devices, or is it typically sufﬁcient to assume that the adversary can only compromise one or the other? ... Can this be leveraged to enact a trust model where the server’s behavior is trusted-but-veriﬁed ... ?

accepted.question_text: Can defenses such as data sanitization and network pruning be adapted to federated learning in a way that does not require direct access to private client data, and how should the gap between data poisoning and model-update poisoning attacks be quantified under realistic federated adversary capabilities?

evidence.quote: Neither data sanitization nor network pruning work directly in federated settings, as they both generally require access to client data, or else data that resembles client data. Thus, it is an open question whether data sanitization methods and network pruning methods can be used in federated settings without privacy loss, or whether or not defenses against data poisoning require new federated approaches. ... One interesting line of study would be to quantify the gap between these two types of attacks, and relate this gap to the relative strength of an adversary operating under these attack models.

accepted.question_text: How can secure aggregation tolerate stragglers and dropouts more gracefully, for example through asynchronous variants or aggregation across multiple rounds, and what general-purpose debugging methods can diagnose federated data-pipeline failures without directly inspecting raw user data?

evidence.quote: Another possibility would be to develop an asynchronous version of SecAgg that does not require clients to participate during a ﬁxed window of time ... More speculatively, it may be possible to perform versions of SecAgg that aggregate over multiple computation rounds. ... Developing general-purpose debugging methods for machine learning that do not directly inspect raw data remains a challenge.

accepted.question_text: To what extent can bias that originates in the data-generating process be detected or mitigated in federated learning, and what methods can apply post-hoc fairness corrections to models learned from potentially biased decentralized interaction data?

evidence.quote: Investigating the degree to which biases in the data-generated process can be identiﬁed or mitigated is a crucial problem for both federated learning research and ML research more broadly. ... Finally, methods for applying post-hoc fairness corrections to models learned from potentially biased training data are also a valuable direction for future work.

accepted.question_text: How can unfairness be measured and corrected in federated settings where sensitive group membership is unavailable, including making approaches such as distributionally robust optimization and multicalibration scale to the large, high-dimensional regime typical of federated learning and developing new theory for fairness without explicit sensitive attributes?

evidence.quote: Both measuring and correcting unfairness in contexts where there is no data regarding sensitive group membership is a key area for federated learning researchers to address. ... The challenge of how to make these approaches work for large-scale, high-dimensional data typical to federated settings is also an open problem ... Finally, the development of additional theoretical approaches to deﬁning fairness without respect to “sensitive attributes” is a critical area for further research.

accepted.question_text: How do client-sampling constraints and decentralized data collection affect fairness in federated learning, and under what assumptions can fairness-improving methods from centralized learning be adapted to the federated setting?

evidence.quote: Future work could investigate the degree to which these various sampling constraints affect the fairness of the resulting model, and how such impacts can be mitigated within the federated framework ... Adapting such solutions to the federated learning setting and further improving upon them will be challenging research questions in ML fairness theory and algorithms. ... It is an open question whether such approaches, which have demonstrated utility for improving fairness in centralized training, could be used under the setting of federated learning ...

accepted.question_text: How should system-induced bias in federated learning be quantified and mitigated in realistic deployments, including through useful proxy metrics, root-cause analysis, stratification strategies, and scheduling or weighting policies?

evidence.quote: While the potential for bias in federated learning has been addressed in the literature ... a systematic study that qualiﬁes and quantiﬁes bias in realistic settings and its sources is a direction for future research. ... We want to encourage further research to study how bias can be quantiﬁed and subsequently mitigated. A useful proxy metric for bias is to study the expected rate of contribution of a device to federated learning.

accepted.question_text: What composite objective functions should be optimized when tuning federated learning systems that must trade off model quality, throughput, convergence speed, fairness, privacy, robustness, and resource use, and how can those settings be tuned automatically rather than manually?

evidence.quote: Deﬁning reasonable composite objective functions, and designing algorithms to automatically tune these settings, has not been explored yet in the context of federated learning systems and hence remains a topic of future research.
